    mssrscopR

    mssrscopR computes single-frame Mean-Shift Super-Resolution (MSSR; Torres-García et al. 2022) structure maps in R. Geometry is explicit, degenerate input has a defined result, and a self-test can check any installation.

    • Compute: mssr() returns the MSSR structure map of one 2D frame, with its role, grid transform, parameters and diagnostics.
    • Locate: mssr_coords() places output pixels in input-pixel coordinates.
    • Select: mssr_mask() derives a structural mask on the input grid for measuring the original data, and reports how much of it tie-breaking decided.
    • Verify: mssr_selftest() recomputes bundled synthetic fixtures.

    Status: 0.1.0.9004, development candidate. At amplification 1 with intensity normalization off, comparisons with the authors’ single-frame R code (disk kernel, rotation undone) and Python code (square kernel) agree on the tested non-degenerate examples. Engine mssr_r_rev3 improves numerical stability; the unchanged bundled synthetic fixtures guard against regressions. Its benefit for fluorescence, histology or hyperspectral analyses has not been established.

    The method concordance in vignette("method-concordance") maps the official supplementary equations to the engine and records implementation differences, unresolved temporal definitions and qualification boundaries (Markdown source).

    Why

    MSSR is easy to run and easy to misread:

    • The authors’ R script returns a rotated image. It fails on non-square frames and returns NaN for flat input.
    • “Amplification” is ambiguous. It adds samples, not observations, and common interpolation grids shift the field of view.
    • The output looks like an image of intensities, but it is not one. MSSR is nonlinear: dim structures next to bright ones are suppressed, and broad or touching objects can be hollowed or split.

    mssrscopR makes each of these explicit: outputs keep the input orientation, coordinates and the field of view are returned with the result, and every result is labeled as a non-quantitative structure map.

    Scope

    In scope

    • Single-frame MSSR of finite 2D numeric matrices of any shape, orders 0–10, integer amplification 1–64 on a field-of-view-preserving grid. This is the accepted syntax; independent qualification covers a bounded subset, and orders above 3 are experimental.
    • Defined results for degenerate input (flat frames, impulses on an exactly zero background), reported in the diagnostics.
    • Structural masks with exact coverage for measurements on the original data.
    • Input validation with classed errors and warnings, resource guards, and an installation self-test.

    Out of scope

    • Temporal MSSR summaries over frame stacks (mean, variance, TPM).
    • Tiled or out-of-core processing: every order step uses image-wide maxima.
    • General-purpose file readers, physical calibration, and claims of resolution gain, intensity fidelity or diagnostic value.

    Where it sits in CTTIR 

    2D frame from any reader (one channel / one band at a time; results of
different channels need not keep their intensity ratios)
      │
      ▼
mssrscopR::mssr()  →  structure map + coordinates + diagnostics
      │
      ▼
mssrscopR::mssr_mask()  →  mask on the input grid
      │
      ▼
measurements on the ORIGINAL frame (your analysis code)

    There are no adapters to other CTTIR packages yet. Use with hyperspectral cubes or segmentation workflows has not been validated.

    Interface

    Function Returns
    mssr(x, fwhm, amp = 1, order = 1, ...) mssr_result: values, role, transform, parameters, engine, diagnostics
    mssr_coords(result) output pixel-center coordinates (row, col) in input-pixel units
    mssr_mask(result, fraction, region = NULL, seed = 1) logical mask on the input grid with coverage, tie_fraction, n_region
    mssr_selftest(tolerance = 1e-10) fixture errors, with attribute all_passed
    mssr_app(max_upload_mb = 50, ...) interactive Shiny explorer (needs shiny, bslib, jsonlite, callr and digest): synthetic examples or an uploaded frame, maps on shared input-pixel axes, profiles, masks measured on the input, self-test, downloads

    fwhm is the point-spread-function width in input pixels and has no default. Errors inherit from mssrscopR_error (subclasses _input, _nonfinite, _parameter, _resource, _unsupported, _numerical, _dependency); negative input gives a mssrscopR_warning_negative warning, because MSSR assumes non-negative intensities, and undefined refinement steps give a mssrscopR_warning_skipped_steps warning.

    Use plain integer or double inputs; explicitly classed numeric objects must be converted deliberately. The engine scales internally and accumulates local differences to reduce overflow, underflow and cancellation. It reports a numerical error if scaling loses a nonzero input or the final output overflows. Very small intensity-weighted outputs remain subject to subnormal rounding, including zero. This cannot recover precision already lost in the supplied frame.

    A constant background changes the result, also for non-negative input: the order-0 structure map does not depend on it, but every refinement step (order >= 1) compares the map with the input divided by its maximum, and intensity weighting multiplies by the input. Subtracting a background is therefore a preprocessing choice that changes the map; record it with the result. The range normalizer adapts to the largest local difference, so even rounding-level ripple on an otherwise flat frame is stretched to full contrast.

    Coordinate and mask consumers check finite values and consistent grid metadata; they do not authenticate image provenance. Positive mask fractions select at least one pixel. tie_fraction is the share of the selected pixels that random tie-breaking among equal scores (usually exact zeros) decided, and cut_relative the lowest selected score divided by the highest. A large tie_fraction or a cut_relative near 0 means the mask reaches beyond the structure that MSSR found, and mssr_mask() warns; choose a smaller fraction or a region. A quota mask is not a cell segmentation.

    Installation 

    # install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("CTTIR/mssrscopR")

    Quick start 

    library(mssrscopR)

# Two blurred point sources 3 pixels apart (FWHM 3 px) on a faint background:
# a shallow dip in the input that MSSR deepens.
g <- expand.grid(r = 1:21, c = 1:25)
spot <- function(r0, c0) exp(-((g$r - r0)^2 + (g$c - c0)^2) / (2 * (3 / 2.3548)^2))
x <- matrix(spot(11, 11) + spot(11, 14) + 0.05, 21, 25)

res <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3, amp = 2)
res
mssr_coords(res)$col[1:4]

# A structural mask on the input grid. Only a few percent of this map is
# positive, so keep a smaller share than that.
r1 <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3)
mean(as.matrix(r1) > 0)          # share of pixels with any structure
m <- mssr_mask(r1, fraction = 0.03)
mean(x[m])                       # measured on the original frame
attr(m, "tie_fraction")          # 0: no pixel was chosen by tie-breaking
attr(m, "cut_relative")          # lowest kept score relative to the highest

attr(mssr_selftest(), "all_passed")

# Explore parameters interactively (needs shiny, bslib, jsonlite, callr and digest):
# mssr_app()

    Relation to the authors’ code

    The authors distribute R, Python, MATLAB and ImageJ code at https://github.com/adanog/MSSR. mssrscopR is an independent implementation and contains none of it. At amplification 1 with intensity normalization off, comparisons agree on tested non-degenerate examples with the authors’ single-frame R function once its final rotation is undone, and with kernel = "square" their Python function. This is a bounded numerical comparison, not a guarantee for every finite input: the revised engine avoids numerical failures of the direct arithmetic at extreme intensity ranges. For flat frames and for impulses on an exactly zero background their R function returns NaN and their Python function returns zeros; mssrscopR returns flagged zeros for flat frames and keeps the map, counting the skipped step, for impulses. With intensity normalization on, their R function multiplies the rotated map by the unrotated input, so it matches mssr() only for frames that a 90-degree rotation leaves unchanged (and fails for non-square frames). Their R mesh compensation shifts asymmetrically (by desp + 1 one way and desp the other); mssrscopR uses the symmetric shifts of their Python code. Amplification uses Keys cubic convolution on a field-of-view-preserving grid, so output for amp > 1 differs from the authors’ interpolation, also with grid = "endpoint", which reproduces their sample positions: pixel-wise agreement is not expected.

    Citation

    Please cite the method paper whenever you use MSSR; citation("mssrscopR") lists it together with the package.

    Use of LLM tools

    Where applicable, LLM tools were used for narrowly defined, non-authorial tasks: copyediting, prose refinement, Markdown/LaTeX formatting, boilerplate scaffolding (such as CI configurations and build scripts), and code refactoring. Tools included Chat AI, the KISSKI (GWDG) service, and self-hosted Mistral Small (24B, Apache-2.0) served through a local vLLM architecture on an Ubuntu Linux workstation with Intel processors and NVIDIA GPUs. The self-hosted model ran locally, with no data sent to third parties.

    All scientific claims, methodological choices, analyses, interpretations and conclusions remain the authors’ own. Where applicable, LLM-generated material must be reviewed and revised before inclusion, and references must be verified against their DOI, arXiv ID or ISBN.

    Local software setup: vLLM with Python/PyTorch, plus R and RStudio.

    Inspect, preserve and resume results

    The development interface adds summary(), plot() and mssr_validate_result() for result inspection. Results carry a separate schema version, engine/package identity and an explicit evidence scope. Unknown acquisition calibration stays unknown; arbitrary matrix attributes are not copied into outputs.

    x <- matrix(seq_len(120), 10, 12)
r <- mssr(x, fwhm = 3, order = 1, max_memory_bytes = 1024^3)
summary(r)
mssr_validate_result(r)
mssr_estimate_resources(dim(x), fwhm = 3)

# Optional packages digest and jsonlite are needed only for file exchange/batches.
# Paths are explicit and output replacement is refused by default.
# mssr_write_result(r, "frame.mssr")
# restored <- mssr_read_result("frame.mssr")
# run <- mssr_batch(list(frame_a = x, frame_b = t(x)), "batch-output",
#                   settings = list(fwhm = 3, order = 1))

    Result files preserve exact binary64 values with SHA-256 integrity checks and bounded, non-executable metadata parsing. Readback establishes consistency, not source authenticity or biological validity. Batch processing is sequential: complete frames, verified reuse, retained failed/cancelled rows and separate attempt files. Cancellation takes effect between frames. The returned table’s run_record attribute identifies the durable invocation summary.

    The allocation model was calibrated on the peak RSS of fresh R processes on one Linux machine over 65,536–16,777,216 output pixels (amplification 1–4, orders 0–3, mesh and weighting on and off, both kernels), where it exceeded every measured peak by 30–220 %, least for order 3 with mesh and weighting. It includes a 128 MiB runtime allowance. Garbage collection, larger workloads, other platforms and retained objects can change RSS; this is not an OS memory cap.

    Recompute a saved result

    mssr_settings() validates a result and returns the eight resolved computation arguments, including its grid. Use it instead of passing result$parameters directly: that field includes the derived half_size and omits the grid. Resolved settings describe what ran; for example, mesh compensation is recorded as off at amplification 1. Resource budgets must be set explicitly for replay.

    # Continue from x and r above; keep the original input separately.
if (requireNamespace("digest", quietly = TRUE) &&
    requireNamespace("jsonlite", quietly = TRUE)) {
  path <- tempfile(fileext = ".mssr")
  mssr_write_result(r, path)
  restored <- mssr_read_result(path)
  stopifnot(identical(restored$engine$package_version,
                      as.character(packageVersion("mssrscopR"))))
  replay <- do.call(mssr, c(
    list(x = x, max_output_pixels = 5e7, max_memory_bytes = 1024^3),
    mssr_settings(restored)
  ))
  stopifnot(identical(replay$values, restored$values),
            identical(replay$transform, restored$transform))
  unlink(path)
}

    This demonstration retains the original input in memory. For a durable analysis, preserve it in trusted storage together with its identity, preprocessing, channel/frame selection, acquisition information, and mask region, fraction and seed. These are not stored in the .mssr result. Preserve the package artifact and runtime environment too. mssr_settings() refuses records from other numerical engines; it does not migrate them. Matching engine/settings alone does not guarantee identical arithmetic across package versions or environments, so compare the recomputed values as above. See the vignette for a worked example that also reproduces the original-data measurement.

    Numerical qualification boundary

    The portable kit in tools/qualification/ evaluates independent high-precision references and keeps failing cases visible. The current bounded core contains 76 passing cases at orders 0–3; this does not establish accuracy for every possible input or parameter combination. Across the wider 98-case sample, two order-10 cases exceed the unchanged tolerance. Small perturbations can be strongly amplified by repeated nonlinear refinement. Orders above 3 therefore produce an explicit qualification warning and remain experimental.

    A small map difference does not guarantee an identical mask: near a cutoff, score perturbations can change selected pixels and measurements made on the original frame. A fixed retained fraction is a quota, not a detector threshold, probability or confidence score. Always inspect retained coverage, cutoff ties, parameter sensitivity and the consequences for the original-data measurement.

    Background app computation

    The app runs one owned background R job per session. Cancel computation stops that job; pending, failed or cancelled work cannot be downloaded. Restore previous completed result recovers the prior input, settings and mask with an explicit restored-state label. Controls edited while a job runs do not change its captured inputs. Current mask controls can update a normally completed result; restored results retain their previous mask settings.

    Jobs stop when the session closes or after five minutes. They inherit CPU constraints and use one numerical thread. The app verifies package files and loaded function definitions in the child, preventing an unnoticed switch to an older installed version. Development-source launches additionally need pkgload; installed packages do not. Dependencies are never installed automatically.

    The app’s Run record uses schema 1.1.0 and includes SHA-256 identities for the uploaded file bytes and decoded frame. It retains neither the filename nor the local path. Keep the source file separately: these hashes establish content identity, not authenticity or acquisition provenance. You can compare the raw file hash with digest::digest(file = "your-frame.csv", algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE).

    The decoded-frame format mssr-input-binary64-v1 hashes this concatenation: the ASCII tag mssr-input-binary64-v1 followed by a newline, two little-endian signed 32-bit integers (row count, then column count), and all finite samples as little-endian IEEE-754 binary64 values in column-major order. Matrix attributes are excluded. Equal decoded frames from different file encodings have the same frame hash, while their uploaded-file hashes can differ.
